{{Short description|Equation in polymer chemistry}}
The '''Mayo–Lewis equation''' or '''copolymer equation''' in [[polymer chemistry]] describes the distribution of [[monomer]]s in a [[copolymer]]. It was proposed by [[Frank R. Mayo]] and [[Frederick M. Lewis]].<ref name=Mayo-Lewis>''Copolymerization. I. A Basis for Comparing the Behavior of Monomers in Copolymerization; The Copolymerization of Styrene and Methyl Methacrylate'' Frank R. Mayo and Frederick M. Lewis [[J. Am. Chem. Soc.]]; '''1944'''; 66(9) pp 1594 - 1601; {{doi|10.1021/ja01237a052}}</ref>

The equation considers a monomer mix of two components <math>M_1\,</math> and <math>M_2\,</math> and the four different reactions that can take place at the reactive chain end terminating in either monomer (<math>M_1^*\,</math> and <math>M_2^*\,</math>) with their [[reaction rate constant]]s <math>k\,</math>:

:<math>M_1^* + M_1 \xrightarrow{k_{11}} M_1M_1^* \,</math>
:<math>M_1^* + M_2 \xrightarrow{k_{12}} M_1M_2^* \,</math>
:<math>M_2^* + M_2 \xrightarrow{k_{22}} M_2M_2^* \,</math>
:<math>M_2^* + M_1 \xrightarrow{k_{21}} M_2M_1^* \,</math>
The '''reactivity ratio''' for each propagating chain end is defined as the ratio of the [[rate constant]] for addition of a monomer of the species already at the chain end to the rate constant for addition of the other monomer.<ref name=Cowie>Cowie, J.M.G. ''Polymers: Chemistry & Physics of Modern Materials'' (2nd ed., Chapman & Hall 1991) p.106 {{ISBN|0-412-03121-3}}</ref>

:<math>r_1 = \frac{k_{11}}{k_{12}} \,</math>
:<math>r_2 = \frac{k_{22}}{k_{21}} \,</math>

The copolymer equation is then:<ref>Fried, Joel R. ''Polymer Science & Technology'' (2nd ed., Prentice-Hall 2003) p.42 {{ISBN|0-13-018168-4}}</ref><ref name=Rudin>Rudin, Alfred ''The Elements of Polymer Science and Engineering'' (Academic Press 1982) p.265 {{ISBN|0-12-601680-1}}</ref><ref name=Cowie/>

:<math>\frac {d\left [M_1 \right]}{d\left [M_2\right]}=\frac{\left [M_1\right]\left (r_1\left[M_1\right]+\left [M_2\right]\right)}{\left [M_2\right]\left (\left [M_1\right]+r_2\left [M_2\right]\right)}</math>

with the [[concentration]]s of the components in square brackets. The equation gives the relative instantaneous rates of incorporation of the two monomers.<ref name=Rudin/>

==Equation derivation==
Monomer 1 is consumed with [[reaction rate]]:<ref>{{cite book|last=Young|first=Robert J.|title=Introduction to polymers|year=1983|publisher=Chapman and Hall|location=London|isbn=0-412-22170-5|edition=[Reprinted with additional material]|url-access=registration|url=https://archive.org/details/introductiontopo00youn_0}}</ref>

<math>\frac{-d[M_1]}{dt} = k_{11}[M_1]\sum[M_1^*] + k_{21}[M_1]\sum[M_2^*] \,</math>
 
with <math>\sum[M_1^*]</math> the concentration of all the active chains terminating in monomer 1, summed over chain lengths. <math>\sum[M_2^*]</math> is defined similarly for monomer 2.

Likewise the rate of disappearance for monomer 2 is:

<math>\frac{-d[M_2]}{dt} = k_{12}[M_2]\sum[M_1^*] + k_{22}[M_2]\sum[M_2^*] \,</math>

Division of both equations by <math>\sum[M_2^*] \,</math> followed by division of the first equation by the second yields:

<math>\frac{d[M_1]}{d[M_2]} = \frac{[M_1]}{[M_2]}  \left( \frac{k_{11}\frac{\sum[M_1^*]}{\sum[M_2^*]} + k_{21}} {k_{12}\frac{\sum[M_1^*]}{\sum[M_2^*]} + k_{22}} \right) \,</math>

The ratio of active center concentrations can be found using the [[steady state (chemistry)|steady state]] approximation, meaning that the concentration of each type of active center remains constant.

<math>\frac{d\sum[M_1^*]}{dt} = \frac{d\sum[M_2^*]}{dt} \approx 0\,</math>

The rate of formation of active centers of monomer 1 (<math>M_2^* + M_1 \xrightarrow{k_{21}} M_2M_1^* \,</math>) is equal to the rate of their destruction  (<math>M_1^* + M_2 \xrightarrow{k_{12}} M_1M_2^* \,</math>) so that

<math>k_{21}[M_1]\sum[M_2^*] = k_{12}[M_2]\sum[M_1^*] \,</math>

or

<math> \frac{\sum[M_1^*]}{\sum[M_2^*]} = \frac{k_{21}[M_1]}{k_{12}[M_2]}\,</math>

Substituting into the ratio of monomer consumption rates yields the Mayo–Lewis equation after rearrangement:<ref name=Rudin/>

<math>\frac{d[M_1]}{d[M_2]} = \frac{[M_1]}{[M_2]}  \left( \frac{k_{11}\frac{k_{21}[M_1]}{k_{12}[M_2]} + k_{21}} {k_{12}\frac{k_{21}[M_1]}{k_{12}[M_2]}+ k_{22}} \right) = \frac{[M_1]}{[M_2]}  \left( \frac{\frac{k_{11}[M_1]}{k_{12}[M_2]} + 1} {\frac{[M_1]}{[M_2]}+ \frac{k_{22}}{k_{21}}} \right) = \frac{[M_1]}{[M_2]} \frac{\left (r_1\left[M_1\right]+\left [M_2\right]\right)}{\left (\left [M_1\right]+r_2\left [M_2\right]\right)}</math>

==Mole fraction form==
It is often useful to alter the copolymer equation by expressing concentrations in terms of [[mole fraction]]s. Mole fractions of monomers <math>M_1\,</math> and <math>M_2\,</math> in the feed are defined as <math>f_1\,</math> and <math>f_2\,</math> where

<math>f_1 = 1 - f_2 =  \frac{M_1}{(M_1 + M_2)} \,</math>

Similarly, <math>F\,</math> represents the mole fraction of each monomer in the copolymer:

<math>F_1 = 1 - F_2 =  \frac{d M_1}{d (M_1 + M_2)} \,</math>

These equations can be combined with the Mayo–Lewis equation to give<ref>Fried, Joel R. ''Polymer Science & Technology'' (2nd ed., Prentice-Hall 2003) p.44 {{ISBN|0-13-018168-4}}</ref><ref name=Rudin/>

<math>F_1=1-F_2=\frac{r_1 f_1^2+f_1 f_2}{r_1 f_1^2+2f_1 f_2+r_2f_2^2}\,</math>

This equation gives the composition of copolymer formed at each instant. However the feed and copolymer compositions can change as polymerization proceeds.

==Limiting cases==
Reactivity ratios indicate preference for propagation. Large <math>r_1\,</math> indicates a tendency for <math>M_1^*\,</math> to add <math>M_1\,</math>, while small <math>r_1\,</math> corresponds to a tendency for <math>M_1^*\,</math> to add <math>M_2\,</math>. Values of <math>r_2\,</math> describe the tendency of <math>M_2^*\,</math> to add <math>M_2\,</math> or <math>M_1\,</math>. From the definition of reactivity ratios, several [[special case]]s can be derived:
* <math>r_1 \approx r_2 >> 1 \,</math> If both reactivity ratios are very high, the two monomers only react with themselves and not with each other. This leads to a mixture of two [[homopolymer]]s.
* <math>r_1 \approx r_2 > 1 \,</math>. If both ratios are larger than 1, homopolymerization of each monomer is favored. However, in the event of crosspolymerization adding the other monomer, the chain-end will continue to add the new monomer and form a [[block copolymer]].
* <math>r_1 \approx r_2 \approx 1 \,</math>. If both ratios are near 1, a given monomer will add the two monomers with comparable speeds and a [[copolymer|statistical or random copolymer]] is formed.
* <math>r_1 \approx r_2 \approx 0 \,</math> If both values are near 0, the monomers are unable to homopolymerize. Each can add only the other resulting in an [[alternating polymer]]. For example, the copolymerization of [[maleic anhydride]] and [[styrene]] has reactivity ratios <math>r_1\,</math> = 0.01 for maleic anhydride  and <math> r_2 </math> = 0.02 for styrene.<ref>Copolymer Reactivity Ratios. ''Polymer Handbook'', 4th ed.; Wiley, '''2003'''; Vol 1, pp 259.</ref> [[Maleic acid]] in fact does not homopolymerize in free [[radical polymerization]], but will form an almost exclusively alternating copolymer with styrene.<ref>Rudin, Alfred ''The Elements of Polymer Science and Engineering'' (Academic Press 1982) p.288 {{ISBN|0-12-601680-1}}</ref>
* <math>r_1 >> 1  >> r_2  \,</math> In the initial stage of the copolymerization, monomer 1 is incorporated faster and the copolymer is rich in monomer 1. When this monomer gets depleted, more monomer 2 segments are added. This is called [[composition drift]].  
* When both <math>r < 1 \,</math>, the system has an [[Composition drift#Azeotropic Compositions|azeotrope]], where feed and copolymer composition are the same.<ref>Rudin, Alfred ''The Elements of Polymer Science and Engineering'' (Academic Press 1982) p.270 {{ISBN|0-12-601680-1}}</ref>

==Calculation of reactivity ratios==

Calculation of reactivity ratios generally involves carrying out several polymerizations at varying monomer ratios. The copolymer composition can be analysed with methods such as [[Proton nuclear magnetic resonance]], [[Carbon-13 nuclear magnetic resonance]], or [[Fourier transform infrared spectroscopy]]. The polymerizations are also carried out at low conversions, so monomer concentrations can be assumed to be constant. With all the other parameters in the copolymer equation known, <math>r_1\,</math> and <math>r_2\,</math> can be found.

===Curve Fitting===

One of the simplest methods for finding reactivity ratios is plotting the copolymer equation and using [[nonlinear least squares]] analysis to find the <math>r_1\,</math>, <math>r_2\,</math> pair that gives the best fit curve. This is preferred as methods such as Kelen-Tüdős or Fineman-Ross (see below) that involve linearization of the Mayo–Lewis equation will introduce bias to the results.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Tidwell |first1=Paul W. |last2=Mortimer |first2=George A. |title=An Improved Method of Calculating Copolymerization Reactivity Ratios |journal=J. Polym. Sci. A |date=1965 |volume=3 |pages=369–387 |doi=10.1002/pol.1965.100030137 |url=https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/pol.1965.100030137 |access-date=14 September 2021|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

===Mayo-Lewis Method===

The Mayo-Lewis method uses a form of the copolymer equation relating <math>r_1\,</math> to <math>r_2\,</math>:<ref name=Mayo-Lewis/>

<math>r_2 = \frac{f_1}{f_2}\left[\frac{F_2}{F_1}(1+\frac{f_1r_1}{f_2})-1\right]\,</math>

For each different monomer composition, a line is generated using arbitrary <math>r_1\,</math> values. The intersection of these lines is the <math>r_1\,</math>, <math>r_2\,</math> for the system. More frequently, the lines do not intersect in a single point and the area in which most lines intersect can be given as a range of <math>r_1\,</math>, and <math>r_2\,</math> values.

===Fineman-Ross Method===

Fineman and Ross rearranged the copolymer equation into a linear form:<ref>Fineman, M.; Ross, S. D. ''J. Polymer Sci.'' '''1950''', 5, 259.</ref>

<math>  G= Hr_1-r_2 \,</math>

where <math> G = \frac{f_1(2F_1-1)}{(1-f_1)F_1} \,</math> and <math> H = \frac{f_1^2(1-F_1)}{(1-f_1)^2F_1}\ </math>

Thus, a plot of <math> H \,</math> versus <math> G \,</math> yields a straight line with slope <math>r_1\,</math> and intercept <math>-r_2\,</math>

===Kelen-Tüdős method===

The Fineman-Ross method can be biased towards points at low or high monomer concentration, so Kelen and Tüdős introduced an arbitrary constant,

<math> \alpha = (H_{min}H_{max})^{0.5} \,</math>

where <math> H_{min} \,</math> and <math> H_{max} \,</math> are the highest and lowest values of <math> H \,</math> from the Fineman-Ross method.<ref>Kelen, T.; Tüdős, F.; Turcsányi, B. ''Polymer Bull.'' '''1980''', 2, 71-76.</ref> The data can be plotted in a linear form

<math>  \eta = \left[r_1+\frac{r_2}{\alpha}\right]\mu - \frac{r_2}{\alpha} \,</math>

where <math>  \eta= G/(\alpha+H) \,</math> and <math>  \mu= H/(\alpha+H) \,</math>. Plotting <math> \eta </math> against <math> \mu </math> yields a straight line that gives <math> -r_2/\alpha </math> when <math> \mu=0 </math> and <math> r_1 </math> when <math> \mu = 1 </math>. This distributes the data more symmetrically and can yield better results.

===Q-e scheme===

A semi-empirical method for the prediction of reactivity ratios is called the Q-e scheme which was proposed by Alfrey and Price in 1947.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Seymour |first1=Raymond |last2=Carraher |first2=Charles Jr |title=Polymer chemistry : an introduction |year=1981 |publisher=M. Dekker |isbn=0-8247-6979-1 |pages=326}}</ref> This involves using two parameters for each monomer, <math> Q </math> and <math> e </math>. The reaction of <math> M_1 </math>
radical with <math> M_2 </math> monomer is written as

<math> k_{12} = P_1Q_2exp(-e_1e_2) </math>

while the reaction of <math> M_1 </math> radical with <math> M_1 </math> monomer is written as

<math> k_{11} = P_1Q_1exp(-e_1e_1) </math>

Where P is a proportionality constant, Q is the measure of reactivity of monomer via resonance stabilization, and e is the measure of polarity of monomer (molecule or radical) via the effect of functional groups on vinyl groups. Using these definitions, <math> r_1 </math> and <math> r_2 </math> can be found by the ratio of the terms. An advantage of this system is that reactivity ratios can be found using tabulated Q-e values of monomers regardless of what the monomer pair is in the system.
